This fundamental fact can be applied to determine the existence of a straight line that intersects every one of the assembled circles exactly once.  This circle-packning conjecture was previously proven under the constraint that no two circles overlap completely, but the current research relaxes this requirement.  Specifically, the research demonstrates that any assemblage of overlapping circles contains a set of three mutually tangent circles that enclose a straight line.  Furthermore, the research provides a numerical value (approximately 0.30) for the minimum ratio of the enclosed straight line's length to the radius of the largest circle in the assemblage.  This value can be seen as a measure of the "tightness" of this specific configuration of overlapping circles, and it can be used as a component in more comprehensive assessments of circle-packings.  It's worth noting that the research assumes all circles have the same radius, and that no four circles share a common point of tangency.  As such, the results of the research can be seen as a refinement of a previous result by R. J. Gardner, rather than a direct proof of the circle-packning conjecture.  In fact, the research can be viewed as a way to approximate the circle-packning conjecture to any desired degree of precision.  For example, if we assume that the smallest ratio of the enclosed straight line's length to the radius of the largest circle in an assemblage of a specific size (e.g. 1024) is at least 0.30, then the results of the research indicate that the conjecture holds true for assemblages of that size or smaller.  In this sense, the research provides a robust way to test the circle-packning conjecture for various degrees of overlap.  In fact, the research can be seen as a way to formulate the circle-packning conjecture in a more precise, quantitative manner.  In this formulation, the conjecture can be restated as the assertion that the ratio of the enclosed straight line's length to the radius of the largest circle in an assemblage of overlapping circles can be made arbitrarily close to 1, given sufficient precision.  As such, the research can be viewed as a demonstration of how testing the circle-packning conjecture for a specific degree of precision can be done by identifying a set of three mutually tangent circles in an assemblage of that precision that enclose a straight line of that precision.

  As the conformal bootstrap approach is mathematically exact, our findings

  Our research focused on conformal theories in two and three dimensions, for
  which we obtained relevant bootstrap conditions that can be used to calculate
  the stress tensor two-point function, including the coefficients of the
  Weyl anomaly-related terms.
  As part of our analysis, we also established a relationship between the
  conformal Ward identity and the conformal bootstrap conditions, which can
  be utilized to infer the two-point function of the stress tensor from the

  effective in determining the stress tensor two-point function once the
  underlying physics is fully captured by the conformal operator algebra. 
  As such, our findings can be viewed as a version of the conformal
  Ward identity that can be utilized to derive the stress tensor two-point
  function from the three-point functions of conformal primary operators. 
  As the conformal bootstrap approach yields an exact result, our findings

  including the associated Weyl anomaly-related terms. 
  As part of our research, we also developed a method for calculating 
  the conformal operator algebra explicitly, which can be utilized to 
  derive the stress tensor two-point function.

  the conformal operator algebra is composed of massless conformal

Current methods either treat age-specific rates as constants or model them using general functions without age considerations. In contrast, we develop a non-parametric regression approach that leverages data on observed incidence and mortality cases to estimate age-specific rates as step functions. This representation facilitates forecasting of age-specific rates and subsequently, the number of new cases and deaths over time. Utilizing our rate estimates, we create a compartmental SIR model with detailed age structure, effectively extending the classic SIR model to incorporate age-specific dynamics. Additionally, we identify the distinct patterns of the 1918 Spanish Flu pandemic in different age groups and forecast the future course of such pandemics. Transfer learning has been a successful approach for reducing the amount of labeling needed, by using pre-trained models on large image classification datasets.  However, using such a broad dataset for object detection training is less effective, because it includes many images that are not relevant to the target scene, thus making the training process less efficient.  Our proposed method, called Dense to RVO, aims to extract a more efficient and targeted set of features from the pre-trained model, by applying a reverse VAT loss in conjunction with a density-based regularization, which enables the model to learn about object density in addition to individual objects.  Additionally, Dense to RVO includes a feature selection mechanism that removes unnecessary features and improves the model's efficiency.  Our experiments show that our method achieves the best results compared to other comparison methods, especially when the target dataset is limited, by using 5 times less data and achieving a mAP of 34\%.  The code and models are available for public use at \url{https://github.com/zhengenhua/D2RVO}. For a one-type branching random walk with a linear drift and a renewal process with a regular tail, we find that the asymptotic distribution of $Z_N$ is governed by the renewal process's tail distribution and the system's geometry, as described by the M\"obius function, which arises from the system's historical configuration. establishing a radio frequency (RF) baseline has become increasingly crucial for subsequent localization methods. This paper introduces a machine learning-based approach to establish an indoor RF baseline in low-power wireless personal area networks (WPANs). Leveraging open-source software-defined radio technology, the authors collected comprehensive real-world RF samples at a high-resolution around multiple indoor paths. A dataset featuring distinct spatial patterns was then extracted from these samples. Using this dataset, machine learning models were trained to differentiate RF signatures associated with various locations within the indoor paths. The results showed that the proposed approach can effectively establish a precise RF baseline in low-PAN WPANs environments. Specifically, the network architecture introduced in this paper, which incorporates a spatial-aware feature extractor, yielded an outstanding accuracy of 99.8% and a modest model size of 0.8 megabytes. Consequently, this research can be utilized as a foundation for developing indoor localization systems that rely on RF baseline data. In such a system, the model can be deployed to generate a precise RF baseline, which can then be employed to recognize new locations within the environment, as demonstrated by an accompanying localization architecture. This eventually led to a precise indoor localization result with only 3 meters standard deviation.

  uncertainties in real-time.

  effects of demand uncertainties and risk in the second stage.
  The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through a case
  study of a test power system with a high renewable energy penetration level. 
  The results show that the robust two-stage stochastic framework can
  efficiently manage power systems with significant renewable energy integration
  and flexible loads, thereby reducing the need for reserve capacity and
  ultimately leading to substantial economic benefits.

  sources of uncertainty and risk in power system management with various

Conversely, we investigate the utilization of classification metrics in image synthesis, specifically focusing on the feasibility of relying on supervised classifiers to differentiate between genuine and fabricated images. We discovered that even relatively basic classifiers can achieve substantial success rates, exceeding 90% in some instances. This phenomenon indicates that, from the perspective of supervised learning, there is a notable distinction between genuine images and those that are fabricated through inversion, capable of being leveraged by simpler, more efficient classifiers. This observation has significant implications for the assessment of supervised image generation methods, implying that we should utilize classifiers that are specifically trained to distinguish between actual and fabricated images, based on visual characteristics, for a more accurate evaluation of such methods. We have established a baseline classifier that you can build upon, utilizing a ResNet-50 architecture, which we called the "Artificial Photographer Detector" (APD). This detector can be employed to evaluate the "photographic authenticity" of images generated through inversion, providing a solid foundation for future research in this domain. We have also clarified the scope of the proposed detector, emphasizing that its primary purpose is to serve as a precise, efficient benchmark classifier for the evaluation of supervised image generation methods, rather than a tool for actual detection of fabricated images. This has already been demonstrated through our experiments, where the proposed detector exhibits significant shortcomings when employed for the actual detection task, as seen in our experiment results. In just one step, the EL method finds an approximate solution.  With an elastic accuracy parameter, it provides solutions bounded by a factor related to the desired level of precision. A mathematical description is created using a one-dimensional model with a moving discontinuity, and we established the global existence and uniqueness of solutions for a reduced problem and the existence of a limited number of solutions for the full problem. Additionally, we discovered that the most unstable eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ can be calculated as the product of two factors: one derived from the edge behavior of solutions, and another, $\sigma_1$(), as the first non-trivial eigenvalue of a specific operator associated with the full problem. Further analysis includes the estimation of $\sigma_1()$ using a modified Loeb's method, and we confirmed that $\lambda_1$ can become negative, leading to the development of a second mode of instability. A similar analysis was performed for a model without a return-to-nuclear-excitation process, and we discovered that this process introduces an additional source of instability associated with electron spin-exchange forces. A numerical computation of $\lambda_1$ was carried out for a specific plasma model, and we confirmed that the most unstable eigenvalue can become positive with an increase in the return-to-nuclear-excitation rate, indicating a shift from a second to a first mode of instability. A discussion is presented on the connection between plasma instability and the return-to-nuclear-excitation process, and we propose that this process could be a driving force powering massive star explosions by causing a second (electron) spin-exchange induced instability of the plasmatic electrosolid dynamics. (OOD) data is crucial for deploying Natural Language Processing models in real-world settings, particularly to prevent the inclusion of misleading or dangerous information in trained models. Existing methods for detecting OOD text primarily rely on machine learning models and incorporate various techniques such as deep neural networks, ensemble methods, and transfer learning. Although these methods have achieved significant success, they can be overly complex and sometimes yield subpar performance on genuine in-domain data. We present a novel, highly effective method called Contrastive Neural Sentence Out-of-Domain Detection, which leverages a comparative learning approach to enhance the uniqueness of in-domain data while maintaining the diversity of OOD data. This method excels above existing approaches and simplifies the subsequent learning task for an classifier. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method by achieving superior results on real-world datasets compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. Code for our approach is publicly available. We establish that for functions exhibiting the image factorization property, the equality of iterates is determined by the value of a finite state machine. These results highlight the significance of the image factorization property in the context of computable mathematics and dynamics. These interactions generate a stream of changing images that the robot observes and responds to, based on past views.  To analyze and learn from such experiences, the robot needs a way to summarize past relevant images, which is equivalent to finding a set of representative points that capture the diversity and pattern of the entire experience.  This challenge can be framed as a novel problem called Diverse and Differential Future (DDF Future), which we propose to address using a unique FutureVisioN network.  This new network consists of multiple diverse future sample modules that ensure the variety of retrieved images, as well as future similarity and temporal coherence modules that maintain the continuity and pattern of the experience.  To efficiently learn from the DDF Future network, we developed a trainable criterion called the Future Retrieval Token Set (FRTS) with a two-stage retrieval process.  To validate the effectiveness of this new framework, we created a comprehensive set of challenging benchmarks called VizWish, which compares favorably to existing datasets in terms of diversity, pattern-based learning, and real-world applications.  The VizWish dataset and rigorous evaluation metrics are accompanied by a state-of-the-art future understanding model called FutureVisioN, which we make available to the public along with the VizWish API and the Diverse Future Retrieval (DFR) toolkit for the benefit of the research community. concept of dark matter has been extensively 
  tested through various astrophysical observations.  Specifically in 
  galaxy-scale studies, researchers have utilized the relationship between 
  galaxy luminosity and dark matter distribution to map the distribution 
  of dark matter in galaxies.  This method has been employed in a range 
  of settings, including the formation of galaxy groups and clusters, 
  large-scale galaxy distributions, as well as the structure of individual 
  galaxies.  Despite its limitations, this approach has been highly 
  effective in providing insights into the interplay between dark matter 
  and luminous matter and has been supported by numerous observational 
  data.  However, the underlying assumption of luminous matter distribution 
  models being accurate needs to be re-examined.  If the properties of 
  luminous matter are found to be influenced by dark matter in a way that 
  distorts galaxy luminosity profiles, then this could introduce a bias 
  into the dark matter maps derived from galaxy luminosity profiles. 
  Interestingly, recent studies have suggested that dark matter could be 
  influencing the properties of luminous matter in galaxies in just this 
  manner, thus potentially introducing a reverse causal relationship 
  between dark matter and galaxy luminosity profiles that needs to be 
  considered in future research.  This potential bias could have a 
  tangible impact on a range of astrophysical and dark matter properties 
  that have been previously estimated.  Therefore, it is crucial to 
  thoroughly assess the impact of this reverse causal relationship on 
  galaxy luminosity profiles before using them to map dark matter in 
  galaxies and to understand the underlying mechanisms governing the 
  distribution of luminous matter in galaxies.  As such, this research 
  proposal aims to explore this reverse causal relationship in detail, 
  specifically by investigating how dark matter influences the scatter 
  of galaxy luminosity profiles and what effect this has on the maps of 
  dark matter in galaxies as well as on estimates of mass properties 
  of galaxy populations.  This proposed research will involve utilizing 
  a combination of galaxy surveys that observe both light and gravity at 
  a variety of scales, including a newly proposed ultra-wide field 
  telescope, in order to refine the models of luminous matter distribution 
  and to directly measure the scatter of galaxy luminosity profiles 
  induced by dark matter.  Additionally, this proposed research will 
  also provide critical insights into the underlying drivers of galaxy 
  luminosity profiles

highly accurate pose estimation models using a large number of objects is addressed.  A major limitation in using object recognition for robot navigation is the substantial training data required, which can't be easily obtain due to the diverse and ever-changing nature of real-world environments.  To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel method, Object-Map Fusion Network (OMFN), that significantly reduces the need for extensive object training.  In the proposed framework, a two-fusion network approach is employed on the target and source data, producing a robust object class recognition model.  The key aspect of OMFN is the incorporation of environmental information in the object recognition model, which is achieved without using any object-related data.  Experimental results show that our proposed method produces a pose estimation model that is highly accurate and requires as little as 8 source images, which is a substantial improvement over the current state-of-the-art methods requiring thousands of images for training.  Additionally, OMFN outperforms the existing models in various challenging scenarios, especially in real-world applications.  We believe our proposed method will serve as a solid foundation for the development of more advanced pose estimation models.  The code and data of OMFN are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengzhengzhai/Object-Map-Fusion-Network.  For the sake of reproducibility and credit, we kindly ask researchers to cite this paper as the original source of this work.  We hope our proposed method will be of great value to researchers working on the problem of object recognition in the absence of large-scale training data.  In order to further evaluate the generalization performance of the proposed method, we conducted an additional experiment by utilizing the MIO dataset, which is a large-scale dataset requiring extensive training data, in comparison with the MSyn dataset that we utilized in the primary experiment, with the aim of verifying the limitations of the proposed method and potential areas for its improvement.  In this supplementary material, we present an expanded version of the MSyn dataset, which we call the Expanded MSyn dataset, with the aim of using it to evaluate the generalization performance of the proposed method.  In this expanded version, we doubled the number of target images and significantly broadened the variety of the source images by utilizing 50 diverse environments.  In this expanded version, we also conducted an additional experiment by incorporating the auxiliary map fusion network in the proposed method, which we call the Enhanced OMFN, with the aim of further enhancing the performance of the proposed method.

  We have developed an image compression model called the Value-Hiding Compression Network (VHCN), which generates compressed images that are suitable for various applications. This model consists of an Encoded Block Model (EBM) and a Feature Extraction Model (FEM), where EBM is used for the initial compression, and FEM re-constructs the crucial image features. We have successfully trained the VHCN model using the CIFAR-10 and MNIST datasets at a 50\% compression rate. Our research indicates that the VHCN model can significantly reduce data volumes without compromising data security. Moreover, our findings demonstrate the VHCN model's capability to obtain valuable information from compressed images. This validates the VHCN model's effectiveness in deriving meaningful data from already compressed images, which is highly beneficial for a wide range of applications that involve the processing of compressed and anonymized data. Such data is commonly used in machine learning models, statistical analysis, and other data processing tasks. Thus, our value-hiding compression framework, along with the VHCN model, provides an excellent solution for issues related to data compression security and the extraction of valuable information from compressed images. 
  We have also conducted an ablation study on the VHCN model's components to determine their importance. Our analysis shows that the Residual Block Model (RBM) is the most critical component of the VHCN model. We have also investigated the impact of varying compression ratios on the VHCN model. Our results indicate that increasing the compression ratio leads to a significant decrease in the accuracy of the machine learning model. However, even at a 50\% compression ratio, the VHCN model is still capable of obtaining valuable information from compressed images.

In this research, we review the methods used to study urban planning information dissemination, focusing on the integration of digital sources into traditional sociotechnical models. Digital sources are viewed as influencing public participation and urban planning policy through various mechanisms. Our discussion highlights the various methods used to study these processes, including policy diffusion, technology adoption, crowd sourcing, social media analysis, and geographic information systems. We also examine the research on digital sources' impact, identifying both positive effects, such as increased public engagement, and negative consequences, like the spread of false information. Furthermore, we review the urban planning projects that have been implemented as a result of digital research, showcasing the tangible outcomes of such studies. Our work serves as a framework for future research on the subject by categorizing the methods used, the urban settings studied, the digital sources examined, and the project outcomes explored. This review also highlights the gaps in current research, such as the lack of studies on low-income cities and the insufficiency of methodological diversification in already studied cities. As such, our work aims to encourage further investigation in these unexplored areas.

As a result, researchers have been working on developing methods to assess the uncertainty of load forecasts, but these efforts have primarily been directed towards modeling the variability of individual forecasts rather than the overall forecast pool used for grid management. In reality, the pool of signed load forecasts used for billing purposes includes both positive and negative forecasts that cancel out, meaning that only the absolute values are utilized. Consequently, the uncertainty of these signed forecasts is overestimated by existing methods. In this paper, we propose a new approach, called the Weibull Distribution Parameter Estimator (WDPE), for determining the uncertainty of signed load forecasts. Specifically, WDPE utilizes a non-parametric estimator to calculate the parameter of a Weibull distribution, which is then used to model the variability of individual signed forecasts. We compare WDPE with alternative methods, including Monte Carlo simulations, and our results show that WDPE provides precise uncertainty estimates while reducing forecasting costs by up to 13% or 100 million dollars annually in a large-scale grid management scenario. has exploded in recent years, with various models being proposed and shown to be highly effective in numerous tasks.  However, the lack of a unified framework to assess different GNN architectures systematically hindered the understanding of their fundamental properties.  To address this gap, we introduced a two-dimensional representation known as the GNN manifold, which facilitates a comprehensive and organized examination of the underlying properties of these models.  The manifold's dimensions are defined by two key characteristics: node pair symmetry and ordering.  We demonstrated how the ordering aspect of the manifold is relevant in relation to node sequence tasks, using a synthetic dataset and the well-known citation network dataset to test different GNN architectures.  The results showed that current GNN assessments are largely based on isolated hypotheses rather than systematic testing, but our findings indicate that the ordering characteristic has a significant impact on the performance of these models.  We also found that ordering-based differences are more pronounced in comparison to pair-specific differences in many cases.  As a consequence of this research, we developed a new GNN model called the Successive Neural Network (SNN), which explicitly addresses the ordering aspect by utilizing a recursive structure.  The results of our research demonstrate that the SNN model performs significantly better in comparison to other GNN architectures that are considered to be of high quality.  The code for the SNN model is available on the GitHub platform.  We also believe that the GNN manifold provides a valuable tool that can be utilized as a foundation for further, more comprehensive research on the properties of GNN architectures.  The methodology and outcomes of this research have implications for the development of more effective GNN models, as shown by our results that the recursive structure-based assessment strategy leads to better performance in comparison to other assessment strategies that are considered to be of high quality.  The code for the synthetic dataset and the citation network dataset processing, as well as the success graph dataset that we created, is available on the GitHub platform under the name gnn-manifold.  We also propose a set of benchmark datasets that we call the ordering-aware datasets, which we believe can be utilized as a starting point for the evaluation of future GNN models that are designed to address the ordering aspect in a more explicit manner.  The code and datasets are available for the benefit of the research community. when a compact object, likely a black hole or neutron star, is orbited by a supermassive black hole.  As the compact object loses mass, the gravitational wave signal becomes more distorted, ultimately leading to its collapse into the supermassive black hole.  Our research focuses on detecting these waves with laser interferometry.  We developed a matched filtering technique to detect these signals and established a minimum signal-to-noise ratio required for detection.  This ratio is expressed in terms of the total energy of the signal and the sensitivity of the detector.  We calculated the detectability of compact objects of varying masses and found that the most promising detections would be for intermediate mass black holes, specifically those with masses between 100 and 1000 times that of the sun, as they emit the strongest signals and have a higher probability of being detected.  However, detecting these intermediate mass black holes will be challenging due to the short duration of their orbital periods which results in a limited amount of data available for analysis.  We determined that in order to detect these intermediate mass black holes we need a detector with a high sensitivity over a wide frequency range which a space-based laser interferometer such as the Big Optical Detector (BOD) would provide, allowing it to detect a larger number of these events during its operational lifetime.  We also found that in order to accurately measure the parameters of these detected signals we need a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 15 which would give a confidence level of 95% for the measurement.  Based on our analysis we estimate that a space-based detector with a bandwidth of 10-200 Hz and a strain sensitivity of 3.8x10^-25/sqrt(Hz) could detect 0.1-10 events of intermediate mass black holes per year.  We propose that a future generation ground-based detector with a high frequency cutoff of 1 kHz could detect a few events of high mass black holes with masses up to 1000 times that of the sun per decade of operation.  In conclusion, detecting these intermediate mass black holes will be achievable in the near future with the development of more advanced gravitational wave detectors and by increasing their sensitivity over a wide frequency range which would significantly improve the probability of their detection and allow for a more accurate analysis of the detected signals.  As such, it becomes feasible to expect the detection of a large number of high mass black hole mergers which would provide invaluable information about their formation and evolution in the early universe. Transfer Learning's success is largely attributed to the similarity between the observation datasets used for training and testing.  However, LfO's primary goal is to handle situations where the observation datasets are fundamentally distinct.  We introduce \codename{Discrete Double Auction} (DDA) for LfO, a novel mechanism that allows a model to be trained on one dataset and subsequently applied to a different, unrelated dataset.  DDA framework consists of a step where models are ranked based on their predicted values, followed by a double auction process that determines which models to select and how much to pay for them.  We prove that the optimal payment for a model corresponds to the difference in future predicted values it generates, which in turn leads to an efficient and scalable algorithm.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of DDA through comprehensive experiments on diverse datasets, showcasing its superior performance compared to current LfO benchmarks.  Notably, DDA's advantages are particularly evident when the observation datasets used for testing are particularly diverse.  We also highlight potential real-world applications of the DDA framework.  We have made the code available for public use.  We hope that the DDA framework will serve as a valuable precursor for the development of more efficient LfO models. To address these obstacles, this paper proposes an innovative full-duplex reconfigurable antenna design that integrates a mm-Wave band and a sub-GHz band within a single device, facilitating seamless frequency switching and minimizing frequency overlap. This method provides a high-resolution spatial distribution of the imaginary part of the permittivity (epsilon''). A one-dimensional imaging model is developed and used to recover epsilon'' by minimizing the difference between the measured phase shift and the predicted phase shift, based on a sparse representation of the permittivity distribution. This results enables us in solving the functional integral challenge of measuring these measures. Particularly for N=2 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory with nilpotent symmetries, we develop a systematic approach to compute the chain equations, measure, and effective action. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the antifield zero mode calculations, previously carried out manually through time-consuming screening techniques, can be automated by implementing the chain equations. Consequently, both measures and effective actions become computable for any N=2 supersymmetric theory, eliminating the need for ad-hoc screening factors. Moreover, we identify the relationship between Witten's open string field theory and N=2 Yang-Mills theory through the presence of a measure that conserves the antifields, allowing us to interpret the latter as a subset of the former. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a more in-depth analysis of N=2 supersymmetric theories through the study of their path space measures. We also propose future lines of inquiry, such as determining the relevance of measure's preservation to the consistency of a theory, as well as exploring the implications of preserving the measure on effective actions.

is proposed for the simulation of Eulerian fluid dynamics. The proposed model is based on a closed system where only the current state of the particle cloud influences the fluid flow. This is in contrast to traditional methods which rely on the past trajectory of the particle cloud to determine the fluid flow. The proposed model includes a statistical tool that ensures an accurate prediction of the fluid flow based on the current particle cloud state. This is achieved by guaranteeing that the model meets the assumptions of the central limit theorem. The effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method are demonstrated through the simulation of a turbulent flow scenario. This is done by using two different models for the prediction of the fluid flow: a nonlinear one and a linear one. The results show that the linear model provides an accurate prediction of the fluid flow and meets the assumptions of the central limit theorem. This is further confirmed by statistical analysis of the data. The efficiency of the proposed method is also shown by comparing it with the efficiency of the Krig method. This comparison reveals that the proposed method has the same efficiency as the Krig method. The effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method are also demonstrated by using different sizes of the particle cloud and different time steps of the simulation. This is done to show that the proposed method can be used for the simulation of complex fluid dynamics without being computationally expensive. The proposed method and its associated challenges are also discussed from the perspective of implementing it using deep learning technology. This discussion highlights the potential of using deep learning to train the proposed method and provide an explicit formula for the prediction of the fluid flow that is based on the current state of the particle cloud. The unique design of the robot allows it to move on multiple surfaces simultaneously, resulting in a high number of possible state combinations that makes traditional method-based learning challenging to achieve meaningful generalization. 

  To overcome this, the TELDE framework leverages learning from diverse experiences through a high-level controller and multiple low-speed child controllers in a closed-loop setting. 

  The paper includes a new method for deriving the set of feasible states for each controller, a control-oriented model inequality approach that utilizes Bernstein's inequality. 

  Additionally, the paper presents a novel state-space learning reward function, a divide-and-conquer state-space partitioning strategy, and a policy learning approach using learning from experience. 

  Validation of the proposed method is carried out through simulation experiments for target reaching tasks on diverse off-road terrain. 

  The results show that the TELDE framework achieves effective state-space learning and target reaching in comparison to a baseline method-based learning approach. 

  The proposed method is further evaluated and validated from a control-oriented modeling perspective.

in stellar convective layers, the method of local shear turbulence simulations has been developed, which allows for a combination with stable triglobal modes of convection. By adopting a triglobal mode configuration, simulations can be achieved that model the overall pattern of convection on the surface of stars and accurately capture the underlying turbulence within the shearing layers. These simulations have been utilized to test the effect of changing surface heat flux on the triglobal mode of convection and subsequently on local shear turbulence. Results have shown that as surface heat flux decreases, the triglobal mode of convection adapts by altering its shear layer thickness, which in turn changes the turbulence characteristics. It has been discovered that the change in turbulence characteristics is closely linked with the rotation of the star and as a result, the solitalian effect that was previously observed is now understood to be a direct result of the changing shear layer thickness rather than a direct effect of the change in angular velocity. Furthermore, it has been found that the change in the thickness of the shear layers does not significantly impact the total turbulent transport in the simulations. Despite this, the effect of changing surface heat flux on the triglobal mode of convection and subsequent change in shear layer thickness does result in a complex interplay between angular momentum transport, changes in the rotation of the star, and the resulting change in the state of the star. As a result, further detailed research is required to fully comprehend the interplay of local shear turbulence with triglobal modes of convection. To this end, an open-source code for the simulation of local shear turbulence in combination with triglobal modes of convection has been made available for the benefit of the scientific community. The code is based on the MAGNETO2-DCA-DIAGT solver and includes additional features such as the Rayleigh-Taylor instability and interface tracking, which allows for the reliable simulation of shearing layers and interface boundaries within the simulations. The code has a modular design that facilitates the exchange of sub-solvers and allows for the incorporation of additional physical processes, such as magnetic field dynamics, which has not been previously modeled in simulations of this nature. The code has a high level of automation that includes the generation of initial conditions, simulation setup, and diagnostics, which includes the analysis of simulations, such as the extraction of triglobal mode properties and the evaluation of turbulent characteristics. The code is executed using the build-and-run system B2R2S and can be run on a variety of high-performance computing architectures, such as Cray XC40 and IBM BlueGene

Interpreting the effects of policy changes, such as lockdowns and mask mandates, requires analyzing data from multiple sources, including transportation records, social media, and reported illnesses. Nonetheless, estimating the parameters of models accounting for many variables, like individual behavior and health conditions, can be computationally intensive for some models, making it hard to handle large datasets. We present a novel statistical method, a stochastic convex polymer model, that efficiently estimates model parameters while adhering to strong mathematical guarantees, thus providing an accurate representation of time-varying relationships. The proposed model exhibits superior performance compared to existing models, as demonstrated by our experiments using real-world data, such as traffic congestion levels derived from Waze and COVID-19 spread data compiled by the World Health Organization. The proposed model has potential applications in rapidly evolving domains where data is plentiful and timely analysis is crucial, such as managing public health systems, transportation networks, and finance systems. The algorithm for the stochastic convex polymer model is scalable and has already been implemented in the Python framework called CEPY. The framework comprises a model class called CEPModel and a set of utility functions for preprocessing data, handling outliers, and managing time-dependent relationships. The best version of the stochastic convex polymer model algorithm was found to be a two-step approach that includes first estimating the parameters of a linear model and then using the polymer model. This approach is efficient and can be done in a batch mode. The algorithm has an established time complexity of O(n^2d) and an estimated time complexity of O(nd^2.67) for certain applications. The proposed algorithm can be run on a typical desktop computer and, as an example, took 3.5 hours to process a dataset of 10 million samples when the number of features was 50. The accuracy of the proposed algorithm was evaluated by conducting experiments on real-world datasets and was found to exhibit superior performance over existing models, with an estimated average gain of 0.25 or more in certain applications. As such, the instrument's ability to identify these signals effectively is paramount. A key challenge in this process is differentiating the signals themselves from background noise, which is comprised of various cosmic and man-made sources of light that could be misinterpreted as genuine gravitational wave signals. In order to overcome this issue, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna will utilize a highly sophisticated optical system on board the satellite to detect and isolate these signals at their source, allowing for the correction of any background noise during the data analysis phase. However, in order to fully comprehend the true nature of these detected signals, it is essential to obtain high-resolution spectral analyses of them. Unfortunately, such analysis is hindered by the satellite's motion and the spread of laser frequencies, resulting in a fundamental limit on the instrument's ability to achieve this goal. In this research, we investigate the impact of the satellite's motion and the spread of laser frequencies on the frequency resolution of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, and explore various signal processing techniques that could potentially enhance the frequency resolution of the instrument. By applying these techniques to simulated data, we demonstrate the feasibility of improving the frequency resolution and point sources discrimination capability of the instrument. In particular, we find that a modest improvement in frequency resolution can be achieved through the use of shorter laser wavelength, and that the application of techniques such as the Short-Time Fourier Transform, Continuous Wavelet Transform, or Neural Networks can significantly enhance the instrument's frequency resolution. These findings suggest that the current frequency resolution of the instrument may already be sufficient for the detection of certain cosmic sources of light that could be considered as gravitational wave signals. As such, the reclassification of such detected signals may be worthy of further consideration in the planning and operation of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna.   computation, before finally conducting a normalized sum of the propagated 
  results. The BEVBP algorithm was found to be significantly more efficient

This method draws inspiration from optimal stable manifold theory and applies it to neural network model compression using the non-convex optimization of over-parameterized networks. This dependence is expressed as a sum of Weyl symbols for the Hamiltonian, with the condition that they satisfy certain Poisson integrals. A key requirement is that a certain operator, representative of the magnetic field, acts correctly on the Weyl symbols, ensuring they accurately represent physical properties. This action of the magnetic field operator on Weyl symbols is in turn defined by the action of its classical counterpart on the underlying classical quantities, as expressed through the Poisson bracket relation.   Silica, a ubiquitous and quantum-stabilizer-friendly material, serves as an

  specific silica-based design that meets both practical requirements and

  silica's $KK$ tensor to safeguard qubits from decoherence-induced errors.

  energy mode at the silica's $KK$ tensor's defect, which can be a reliable
  source of error correction codes, allowing for the development of quantum
  devices utilizing silica surfaces. Importantly, this prediction can be tested
  experimentally using $KK$ tensor-based simulations with an infinite-range
  Ising model, incorporating defect degrees of freedom. Ultimately, the BeBAC

  feasible, silica-based solution for quantum stabilizer technologies.

Our research reveals distinct string profile formations in two scalar field models commonly studied, including the "neutron star-like" profile in a single condensate and a "crust-like" profile in a oscillating condensate scenario. A theoretical explanation is provided for the "crust-like" profile, involving a rotating frame of reference to describe the interaction between the strings and the surrounding matter, and it's shown how this approach can be applied to various potential configurations by combining and scaling individual components. in data-driven character animation, where a virtual actor is manipulated to mimic another character's movements. This process generally requires significant time and expertise. Our proposed technique, called a Performance Primal Sketch (PPS), streamlines this process by condensing another actor's animation data into a simplified representation, which can then be easily modified to match the desired character. 

  Unlike typical methods that rely heavily on computer animation simulations and vast character databases, PPS builds upon fundamental concepts from computer graphics to create a more efficient solution. It begins by reconstructing the target character's 3D surface and skinning system through a process called projection-based reverse engineering. This allows for the generation of a compact, two-part database: a basic character template with associated deformation details. 

  These databases serve as the core components of the Performance Primal Sketch, which is represented as a minimal set of control points that map to specific locations on the character template and corresponding orientation and pen weights that define the shape and features of the target character. 

  The next step in the PPS process involves aligning the performance capture data with the projected character surfaces and binding the data to a compact, two-part character database through a mechanism called the Splat Tree. 

  This enables the creation of a Performance Primal Sketch, which can be achieved by minimizing a Coons patch that fits the bounded surface and determining the pen weights and orientation of the patch. 

  Our research includes two main extensions: transferring cloth animation and handling complex character surfaces. 

  In the case of cloth animation, we apply a strategy of reducing complex patterns to their most fundamental components, whereas a technique called Reconstruct Procedural Assets is utilized to create a set of procedural rules governing the character surface, which can then be combined with the PPS framework. 

  These combined elements can be easily combined and modified to match the desired character through the manipulation of the Performance Primal Sketch. 

  As for handling complex character surfaces, we propose a method of dividing such surfaces into simpler components and associating these components with specific parts of the Performance Primal Sketch, which can then be easily merged to recreate the original surface. 

  We test our technique on a variety of scenarios and demonstrate that it yields results superior to existing methods in terms of accuracy, while also offering the benefit of enhanced editing flexibility.

Notably, these representations can be viewed as variations of the original definition, effectively establishing the equivalence between Fox-Hartwig hypergeometric functions and conventional hypergeometric functions. This equivalence is characterized by the application of a specific change of variables, which we call the Fox-Hartwig transformation. The transformation is particularly useful for expressing mathematical objects of interest as Fox-Hartwig hypergeometric functions, thereby conferring on these objects the desirable properties inherited from conventional hypergeometric functions. The method we introduce is accompanied by an example that involves the construction of a set of orthogonal polynomials, specifically the ultraspherical polynomials. The underlying principle we employ is the recognition that any relationship between mathematical objects of interest can be reframed in terms of the Fox-Hartwig transformation, thereby establishing the equivalence between the original and transformed objects. The transformation is derivable through a sequence of elementary transformations that can be realized using the properties of conventional hypergeometric functions, including their defining differential and integral equations. The underlying idea we introduce can be applied to a broad range of mathematical objects of interest, as illustrated by the derivation of representations for the coefficients of Heine's basic hypergeometric series and the ultraspherical polynomials. The method we present is also viewed as a means of extending the concept of the gamma function to non-integer values, as evidenced by the derivation of representations for the Fox-Hartwig hypergeometric functions in the context of complex analysis. The method we introduce is further seen as a tool for identifying the underlying structure of diverse mathematical objects of interest, as illustrated by the recognition that the Askey-Clensons operator factorization can be viewed as a result of applying the Fox-Hartwig transformation to the associated set of orthogonal polynomials. To evaluate the potential of the MHTC-20 corpus, we conducted a series of experiments using machine learning models that incorporated various annotation categories and assessed their impact on model performance. The MHTC-20 corpus is a newly developed and freely available dataset that is suitable for a wide range of NLP tasks related to mental health, including the detection of positive, negative, and neutral sentiments, as well as the identification of self-harm and suicidal texts. cuprates are intricately related to their angular anisotropic in-plane
ferromagnetic dipolar fields, and how these in-plane fields influence
electrons with little spin-orbit coupling is now being intensely studied
and debated.  Two possible in-plane magnetic field distribution scenarios
have been proposed: a highly anisotropic "ornamental" field pattern 
with $c$-axis oriented field that could be derived from three-dimensional
magnetic ordering, in contrast to a more symmetric "ring-shaped" field 
pattern that would indicate in-plane ordering.  We propose a novel 
method using magnetotransmission modulation spectroscopy to directly 
investigate the in-plane magnetic field distribution and thus determine 
the nature of magnetic ordering in electron systems of cuprates.  Our 
prediction also identifies potential transmission modulation features for 
different ordered states and magnetic field orientations, and shows 
how, even with limited experimental data, the transmission modulation 
spectrum can be reconstructed, and thus how further experimental evidence 
can be obtained to support or refute this proposal.  One of the main 
consequences of this proposal is that transmission modulation spectroscopy 
is sensitive to the spatial distribution of the in-plane electron system' 
magnetic field, which could be a critical benefit for understanding 
how the quasi-two-dimensional electron system's magnetic properties are 
influenced by their surrounding three-dimensional magnetic ordering.  We 
also outline potential applications for this proposal-based methodology

system's magnetic field in cuprates, and present potential experimental 
and theoretical directions for further research.  In conclusion to this

spectroscopy can play in unraveling the complex relationship between the 
quasi-two-dimensional electron system's magnetic properties and their

Our analysis aims to explore the impact of a scalar confining symmetry, a key feature of quantum chromodynamics, on dark energy evolution. We establish that the entropy of dark energy is conserved in a specific way, which results in an evolving scalar component that matches $R^2$ gravity. A similar analysis is also performed for $F(R)$ gravity, showing that the condition of a single power of the curvature scalar $F'(1)=1$ leads to the conservation of entropy associated with the dark energy and, as a consequence, the recovery of $R^2$ gravity. We further investigate these theories by applying them to the observed evolution of the universe and find that to match observations, the fundamental theory of general relativity must be modified in such a way that the acceleration of the universe is attributed to the scalar component, which, in turn, is caused by the time-dependent violation of the fundamental theory of general relativity. We validate our models by fitting their parameters to data available up to the present day and find that to the accuracy of our calculations, the decay rate of the fundamental freedom of general relativity is indistinguishable from a constant. We estimate this constant as $0.016\pm0.045$ per Gyr, whichcorresponds to a timescale of $62\pm18$ Gyr for the onset of the acceleration of the universe. We also estimate the timescale of the variation of the scalar component as $3.4\pm1.5$ Gyr, which indicates that the acceleration of the universe can be attributed to a failure of the fundamental theory of general relativity rather than the properties of dark energy itself. We believe that our study provides a meaningful extension to existing models of the evolution of the universe and offer it as a viable explanation for the acceleration of the universe that is distinct from dark energy. We support this study with numerical data available in the appendix. We stress that due to the limitations of our linearised analysis, any detection of the parameter $0.016\pm0.045$ would, in fact, be evidence for the failure of the fundamental theory of general relativity rather than an increase in the acceleration of the universe. We propose that future research should be directed towards an extension of our models that takes into account the nonlinear aspects of general relativity in order to enhance our comprehension of the failure of the fundamental freedom of general relativity at large scales. physical objects placed in the field of view of a computer camera have a high potential for being used in real-world security breaches.  Against the backdrop of increasing accessibility of 3D printing technology, it's crucial to assess the capabilities of models used in the development of these attacks.  In the realm of deep learning, 3D spatial spreading attacks have been shown to achieve a high success rate even when the target model is not aware of the physical environment in which the image is being captured.  It's essential to understand that these attacks are highly portable and can withstand changes in lighting conditions, the distance between the camera and the subject, and the orientation of the object being targeted.  As for the spreading attacks that use 3D models captured by the adversary, it's necessary to assess existing defenses and to explore more robust methods of detecting these attacks during image capture, without the need for access to training data.  In this research, we are filling a significant gap in the study of adversarial patch attacks that incorporate 3D spatial spreading, by providing researchers with pre-printed 3D objects that can be used in the development of these attacks, as well as a detailed framework for the spreading attack that uses 3D models captured by the adversary, which can be employed in various applications such as security testing of computer models used in the development of deep learning models.  As for the detection of these attacks, we propose a category of detection methods that we call physical regularizers that incorporate 3D spatial spreading, which includes a deep learning-based detector that we call the 3D Spatial Spread Detector (3DSSD).  The 3DSSD detector is a two-stage detector that first identifies the location of the object and then verifies its presence by analyzing the features of the 3D object.  We also propose a category of detection methods that we call data-driven regularizers that incorporate 3D spatial spread, which involves training a separate detector on data that includes 3D objects.  We tested the 3DSSD detector on the spread data that we captured, as well as on new, unseen data, and the results show that the 3DSSD detector is effective in detecting 3D spatial spread.  As for the 3DSSD detector, we are making it publicly available along with the pre-printed 3D objects and the code for the 3D Spatial Spread Detector, in the hope of facilitating further research in this domain. A decentralized optimization approach has been established for solving the offline version of DJSSP, utilizing a bilevel programming framework that takes into account the competitive nature of machine-task assignments. However, this approach requires solving a difficult subproblem for each decision-making period. This study introduces a new algorithm called Decentralized Feasible Sequencing (DFS), which determines feasible sequences for each machine by prioritizing task selection based on their potential processing times and the remaining free time on the machine. DFS demonstrates improved performance compared to the existing decentralized algorithm, specifically showing increased system throughput by 14.7% in an extensive simulation experiment. Additionally, DFS's marginal cost is relatively low, making it suitable for various applications. The proposed approach has implications for decentralized scheduling protocols and provides a practical solution for industrial applications. The underlying model can be seen as a generalization of problems such as the job shop scheduling problem, assembly line balancing problem, and flow shop scheduling problem, all of which involve determining machine-task assignments. The key distinction here lies in the absence of dead lines in the model, making it challenging to optimize. The proposed DFS algorithm can be used as a post-processing step to improve the efficiency of existing solutions for the aforementioned problems by arranging tasks on machines in a feasible and efficient manner. The performance gain achievable through the use of DFS is problem-dependent; nonetheless, in the model studied here, it yields notable outcomes. The Decentralized Feasible Sequencing algorithm exhibits a relatively high computational overhead; nonetheless, the duration required to compute a sequence is significantly lower than the duration of a decision-making period. Consequently, it is advisable to compute multiple sequences in advance and choose the most suitable one based on the predicted free time on machines during each period. The required additional memory to store precomputed sequences is relatively modest, as illustrated by the results presented here, which involve storing 20 sequences for a 10-period window, necessitating approximately 800 bytes of memory. The computational cost and the memory needed to store precomputed sequences provide incentives to explore alternative algorithms with a lower computational cost. To adhere to these standards, range operators must balance the safety of shooters with the necessity to comply with outdoor noise limitations. In this research, our primary objective is to identify cost-efficient strategies for managing outdoor shooting ranges to minimize noise pollution while ensuring shooter safety. We developed a mathematical model to achieve this goal, considering the placement of targets at varying distances to balance noise levels and shooter safety. Utilizing our model, we explored different policies for target placement and analyzed their impact on noise levels, shooter safety, and operational costs. We also established conditions for optimal target placement and explored the implications of these conditions on noise levels, shooter safety, and operational costs. In particular, we found optimal target placement patterns and demonstrated how these patterns could be achieved through the repetition of simpler patterns. We also introduced a randomized strategy for setting target distances and validated its effectiveness theoretically. In addition, we identified the potential benefits of limiting the maximum allowed sound levels to 85 dBA at 50 meters from the shooter, found optimal intervals for repositioning targets, and explored the consequences of doing so. Due to the lack of a comprehensive database specifically for the Swiss Platform (SP) at an altitude of 3600 meters above sea level, a mobile measurement device was created to take readings in the mountain environment. The device, featuring a polyethylene block to slow down cosmic particles, includes a 1-meter$^2$ surface area and can detect the effects of GCRs on equipment via light-emittance, voltage fluctuations, and memory failures in digital components. The research aimed to quantify the impact of GCRs on electronic systems at high altitudes by measuring the associated light emission, and to compare these results with those obtained at lower elevations in the Swiss Alps. The mobile measurement device recently used near the Swiss Platform yielded an average radiation intensity of approximately 0.34 GSE per hour, demonstrating a moderate level of GCR influence at high altitudes that can be easily counteracted with conventional electronics protection methods.  The easy implementation and relatively low-cost of the mobile measurement device used in this research make it a useful model for other scientists and researchers who wish to monitor GCRs in various environments. The simple device features a compact size, weighs approximately 50 kilograms, and can be operated using a battery power source for extended periods, facilitating its use in a wide range of environments and settings for the purpose of GCR detection and related electronic component failure analysis. The results obtained from the mobile measurement device in the Swiss Alps provide a comprehensive understanding of the impact of GCRs at high elevations and can be utilized to develop more accurate testing and simulation environments for electronic components and systems that operate in similar conditions.  Further research is needed to comprehensively pin down the variables influencing GCRs in the Swiss Alps, such as atmospheric pressure, humidity, and temperature, as well as to investigate the effects of GCRs on digital components and systems over an extended period using a more comprehensive testing setup that includes memory chips. A key component of  this theory involves establishing that the optimization maximum of the regularized  logistic regression function equals the optimization maximum of the regularized  log-likelihood function, which can be achieved under a condition of sparse,  nonzero parameters and a sparse, nonzero data distribution. However, there is a limitation to this method as it cannot break down the underlying processes of the solar plasma that give rise to the emission. As a result, the true nature of the emission, whether it's from the 1500 Kelvin reservoir or the 10 million Kelvin core, remains unclear and requires further analysis. Our research utilizes the non-LTE resonance line formation theory to model the observation of the O IV 808 Angstrom line and demonstrates how the same line can be formed in both the corona and the chromosphere. It also identifies the challenges of accurately interpreting the data and the potential for testing the validity of these models through high-resolution observations. By studying this specific line, we have found a correlation between the appearance of the O IV 808 Angstrom line in the spectrum and the footpoint activity of the magnetic loops within the solar atmosphere, with the line only appearing in the spectrum when there is footpoint activity. This correlation can be seen in both the spatial distribution of the emission and the change in intensity over time during a solar flare event. It is worth noting that the relationship between the return of the emission in the O IV 808 Angstrom line and the return of the footpoint activity of the magnetic loops can be used as an indicator of when the energy released during a solar flare event has reached the surface of the Sun and as such can be utilized in the estimation of the mass and energy expelled during an event. The clique cover of a graph is the smallest number of cliques needed to cover the vertex set of the graph. We show that for any connected simple graph without triangles, its $\omega$-index, clique cover, and number of vertices are related by the formula $\omega(G)\leq \frac{\omega(G)+\triangle(G)}{2}$ holds, where $\triangle(G)$ denotes the maximum degree of the graph. Furthermore, this inequality can be tightened to $\omega(G)\leq \frac{\omega(G)+\triangle(G)}{2}+\varepsilon$ for any connected bipartite graph without triangles, with $\varepsilon$ being an arbitrarily small positive number. We also demonstrate that the ratio $\frac{\omega(G)+\triangle(G)}{2}$ can be used as a clique cover approximation with a two-thirds precision for any connected simple graph without triangles. As a corollary, we obtain the verifiable conclusion that the $\omega$-index of any star-free graph can be determined as either 2 or 3. We further establish that the ratio $\frac{\omega(G)+\triangle(G)}{2}$ is almost a clique cover approximation for any connected simple graph without triangles to the power of $n$, with $n$ being an arbitrarily large number. Additionally, we find that the ratio $\frac{\omega(G)+\triangle(G)}{2}$ is a precise clique cover approximation for specific families of graphs, including trees and forests, as well as series-parallel graphs. Moreover, we establish that the calculation of the $\omega$-index to the power of $n$ or the calculation of the ratio $\frac{\omega(G)+\triangle(G)}{2}$ for a graph generalizes to an $n$-step process. We also discuss the computational complexity of the $\omega$-index calculation to the power of $n$ or the ratio $\frac{\omega(G)+\triangle(G)}{2}$ calculation for a graph and we show that this process is computationally complex and, in fact, it is at least as complex as the calculation of a maximum clique in a graph. This particular Finsler manifold can be thought of as having three distinct properties: (1) local expression - a change in coordinates that maintains direction will result in a new expression that only depends on the original direction; (2) positive flag function - a non-negative function that equals zero at the origin and is homogeneous of degree one in its argument; (3) compact support. Under these conditions, we find that geodesics on the manifold can be identified as straight lines, and we also establish that any continuous, orientation-preserving map from a line segment to the manifold has a specific property - its local expression is only dependent on its starting direction. This fact can be used to demonstrate the existence of a unique geodesic between two given points on the manifold, and this geodesic is described as the image of a specific parameterized line segment under the continuous, orientation-preserving map. In particular, if the map in question is a projection, then the geodesic between two points on the manifold can be thought of as the shortest path between those two points. We also examine the situation in which the flag function is not only non-negative but also non-zero, and in which the Finsler manifold has a 4d representation rather than a 3d representation. In these cases, we find that geodesics can be determined as straight lines, and we establish conditions under which this is true.   size means that its crater Berberich, which was previously

In contrast to individual models, the parameters and workings of ensemble models are not well understood, and there is a lack of methodologies to decode the knowledge contained within them.  In this paper, we introduce a new concept of ensemble overfitting that is distinct from traditional overfitting and is characterized by the degradation of ensemble performance when activated by the addition of noise.  We discovered that this phenomenon is caused by the ensemble models sharing identical loss functions but having distinct optimal parameter values, which leads to the creation of a high-dimensional equilibrium where the gradients of the loss function are zero.  Based on this insight, we developed an iterative decoding algorithm that can be used to obtain the ensemble's shared knowledge in the form of noise.  Furthermore, we found that this noise is not random and can be utilized to enhance the ensemble's performance by training a resiliency model that is capable of withstanding the effects of this noise.  In our experiments, we demonstrated the efficacy of this approach for a wide range of deep learning models, including NLP tasks such as language models and text classification, as well as CV tasks such as image classification.  We have made our code publicly available. The problem is challenging due to the variety of possible layouts and the limited information available to developers about the final application window. To address this issue, a new approach is proposed that utilizes a bilevel optimization model to position components, with the outer optimization model representing the GUI development process and the inner model reflecting the window layout. The feasibility of this approach is demonstrated through a set of experiments using a proposed pseudo-force field simulation algorithm. The results show that the proposed algorithm achieves efficient and accurate results, even with a limited number of simulation iterations. The paper also presents a case study showing the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in handling complex and overlapping component interactions. A preliminary evaluation of the algorithm's performance highlights its fast simulation capability, while a more comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm is provided in the appendix. A possible implementation of the algorithm as a plugin for an existing GUI builder is also presented. 

  The paper's main contributions can be summarized as follows:
  1.  A new bilevel optimization framework for GUI component placement is introduced.
  2.  A pseudo-force field simulation algorithm is proposed to solve the optimization problem efficiently.
  3.  The effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm are demonstrated through a set of experiments. 

  The paper's results provide a starting point for further research along this line, specifically in enhancing the proposed algorithm's capability to handle diverse, non-rectangular component layouts.

It is known that the answer lies somewhere between three and four ports, but an optimal solution has yet to be found. This study focuses on the creation and testing of a language to express assembly problems of this type, allowing for a novel approach to one of the port configurations recently proposed as a lower bound for this specific assembly problem. In addition, it is demonstrated that a particular two-port configuration, which involves placing tiles on either side of a central line, is equivalent to a specific type of three-dimensional sorting problem known as "stacking with removal from the top". As such, it cannot have fewer than three ports and is therefore not a viable candidate for the optimal solution to the planar assembly problem involving 1x2 tiles. In this paper, a new pruning method called Progressive Compressed Sensing (PCS) is presented, which starts by identifying the most important neurons by measuring the magnitude of their output, and then eliminates less significant neurons in subsequent iterations. The PCS method determines the optimal number of remaining neurons as the number that yields the lowest error rate while meeting the required accuracy threshold, which is determined using compressed sensing techniques. Experimental results on multiple datasets show that PCS outperforms traditional equal-magnitude sparse activation (ESM-SA) equally or by up to 13\% in terms of the number of neurons required to achieve a similar level of performance. The PC-S algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness are further highlighted by the rapid processing time required to find the optimal sparse configuration for big data datasets. The proposed PCS algorithm's main and auxiliary optimization problems are formally proven to be convertible into integer forms, guaranteeing that the model can achieve the optimal solution. The PC-S algorithm is tested on big data datasets and shown to process them quickly, with an average processing time of 13 seconds for a dataset of 50,000 samples, and is therefore an efficient and effective sparse model initialization method. The proposed PCS algorithm achieves state-of-the-art results in multiple datasets and is therefore recommended as a reliable sparse model initialization method. However, traditional one-way data network models have been primarily studied, leading to a lack of research on two-way data networks.  A new two-way data network model has emerged, characterized by multiple access networks where multiple devices share the same bandwidth to transmit data to a central hub.  This model features controllable reciprocity in communication, which allows the central hub to obtain aggregated linear representations of incoming data through a linear transformation at the receiving end.  The aim of this paper is to establish connections between the new two-way data network model and existing one-way data network models, specifically to generalize results from one-way networks to the new two-way model.  The paper introduces a new concept, Output-Constrained Multiple-Access (OCMA), which includes output-restricted Multiple-Access (MRCA) as a subset, and explores its implications to better understand the new two-way data network model.  The paper also investigates diverse linear receiver techniques within the framework of OCMA and provides recovery guaranties using the new uniqueness and identifiability conditions, which can be viewed as generalizations of unique and identifiable one-way data networks.  The paper provides detailed analysis on diverse network configurations such as blind sparse recovery, Compressed Sensing, and Overdetermined Identifiable, as well as a discussion on various receiver techniques including blind and non-blind sparse, Compressed, and Deterministic.  The paper also offers implementation guidelines for the development of apps that can efficiently manage large-scale multiple-access data collections at the hub.  The paper formally introduces output-constrained multiple-access and output-restricted multiple-access as new uniqueness and identifiability conditions, which can be viewed as generalizations of unique and identifiable one-way data networks, and provides detailed discussion on diverse receiver techniques that can be used under these conditions, including but not limited to sparse, Compressed, and Deterministic receivers.  The paper further explores output-constrained multiple-access to derive output-constrained signal models that can be used to design receiver techniques that can efficiently decode the original signals from the aggregated linear representations with the output constraint. fundamental challenge in genomics.  To address this issue, researchers have been using genetic interactions to map functional relationships and determine the functions of genes.  However, these interactions are often influenced by factors such as environmental conditions, age, and sex, which can impact their relevance for interpreting genomic data.  To deal with this variability, researchers have been looking for methods to identify general, or "conserved", genetic interactions that remain stable across different situations and have a significant impact on gene function.  To this end, researchers developed an approach, called DISCO, which uses machine learning to pinpoint long-lasting, universal genetic interactions and distinguish them from shorter-lived, isolated ones.  This was demonstrated by applying DISCO to yeast, resulting in the mapping of 6,500 high-value, general genetic interactions for 5,800 yeast proteins.  Furthermore, this set of general interactions was found to be valuable for predicting new interactions, identifying genes with similar functions, and analyzing complex biological conditions.  The calculated interactions also provided a clear, quantifiable explanation for why many variability-driven genetic interactions exist and how they are influenced by factors such as age and specific environmental conditions.  The developed approach, along with the obtained data, is available under the name DISCO for the research community to use and apply to other organisms. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed to estimate perceived performance metrics from low-level system behavior using a theoretical model of user perception. The model is based on the concept that the perception of performance is primarily influenced by the response time of a application's user interface, which in turn is affected by CPU usage. The proposed estimation algorithm utilizes this understanding and the non-linear relationship between CPU usage and the response time, as predicted by the standard ITX model. Furthermore, to enhance accuracy, the proposed model is implemented as a reachability-based testing strategy that leverages the estimated metrics and system behavior to determine reachable states corresponding to particular performance outcomes, ultimately leading to the creation of test cases that confirm the predicted outcomes through real-world experiments. Experimental results validate the proposed model's performance and predictivity, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed testing strategy. To facilitate widespread adoption, the proposed model has been integrated into an automated testing framework that is openly accessible.
